# Contract Manufacturer Outreach Package — reusable template

A founder-facing package for taking a consumer brand from small-batch or hand production into
commercial contract manufacturing. Built for VGP advisory and Brand Blueprint coaching engagements
and reused across categories (skincare, oral care, food, supplements).

> **This repo is public.** Nothing below names a founder, a brand, a manufacturer contacted on a
> founder's behalf, a price, a margin or a volume from a live engagement. Fill those in from the
> client folder at build time; never commit the filled version. See the data-handling rules in
> [`docs/prompts/client-engagement-operations.md`](../prompts/client-engagement-operations.md).

---

## When to use it

A founder is producing by hand or in small batches, has real demand evidence (a retail door, a
repeat DTC base, a wholesale enquiry), and manufacturing capacity is the binding constraint on the
next stage of growth. That is the moment. Earlier than that, the package produces conversations the
founder cannot convert.

**Do not open it when** the founder has no demand signal, or when the product formulation itself is
still being decided. A contract manufacturer conversation costs credibility if the brand cannot say
what it wants made.

## What the package contains

Five pieces, built and delivered together as one client-facing document plus a separate product brief.

| # | Piece | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Outreach email template | First contact. Copy-paste, fill a small number of named blanks, send. |
| 2 | The blanks, and where each answer comes from | Turns the template into something the founder can finish alone. |
| 3 | Follow-up email | One nudge at five business days. Produces most of the replies. |
| 4 | First-call guide | What to ask live, and what a good answer sounds like versus a worrying one. |
| 5 | Weighted evaluation scorecard | Forces comparison on the same terms rather than on rapport. |

Plus, as a separate deliverable: a **product brief** the outreach email explicitly promises.

---

## The two preconditions

Both change the content of the email. Neither is optional, and both are cheap.

1. **Target retail price points must exist first.** Until the founder has walked the shelf their
   product is going onto — or an equivalent shelf in the target channel — and recorded competitor
   prices, they can only ask a manufacturer *"what does it cost?"* That is the weak version of the
   conversation. The strong version is *"here is the shelf price I have to hit and the landed cost
   that implies — can you get there?"* Shelf price, less retailer margin, less brand margin, is the
   landed-cost ceiling. Recon precedes outreach.

2. **The longlist must be cut to four or five.** Founders who run ten live manufacturer
   conversations alongside a job stall out. Cut on regulatory posture and minimum order quantity
   first, cost last. At low opening volumes a small MOQ and a pilot option are worth more than a few
   cents of unit cost.

---

## 1 · The outreach email

**Subject:** `Contract manufacturing inquiry — <category>, <n> SKUs, retail-ready run`

```
Hello,

I'm <FOUNDER NAME>, founder of <BRAND>, a <CATEGORY> brand based in <CITY, STATE>. We are moving
from small-batch in-house production into commercial contract manufacturing, and I'd like to find
20-30 minutes with the right person on your team.

WHERE THE BRAND IS

<Two to four sentences: what the line is, how it sells today, and the demand evidence that makes
this real — a retail door opening, anchor accounts converting, a wholesale enquiry. Name the
constraint plainly: everything we sell today is produced by hand, and that is what we are solving.>

WHAT WE'RE LOOKING TO BRIEF

- <n> SKUs in retail-ready packaging: <formats>, with fill sizes and components sized for
  <the target channel>.
- An opening production run of <volume range>, with the ability to scale as distribution grows.
- <Formulation posture — e.g. natural, botanical-forward, clean-ingredient. State that formulation
  fidelity matters more than shaving the last cents out of unit cost, if that is true.>

We're approaching you because <ONE SPECIFIC REASON — see below>.

WHAT I'D LIKE TO COVER ON A CALL

1. What do you need from us to produce a product brief and an initial quote per SKU?
2. Minimum order quantities, per SKU and per production run, and whether they change on reorders.
3. Do you source packaging and components, or do we bring them to you?
4. Formula ownership — who holds the IP if we develop a formulation with you and later move
   production.
5. Your sampling and pilot-run process, and what it costs.
6. Realistic lead time from approved brief to first production run.

<Category-specific additions go here — see "Category add-ons" below.>

We have a written product brief ready to share under NDA, including target fill sizes, volume
assumptions and cost targets, so you would not be starting from a blank page.

Would sometime in the next week or two work? Send a few windows and I'll make one of them work.

Best regards,
<FOUNDER NAME>
<TITLE, BRAND>
<PHONE>
<EMAIL>
<WEB>
```

### The six questions are fixed

Every manufacturer gets the same questions in the same order. When the answers come back they line
up side by side instead of becoming several conversations that have to be translated. This is what
makes the scorecard work, and it is the one part of the template the founder should not rewrite.
Everything else — voice, length, ordering of the narrative sections — is theirs to change.

### Category add-ons

Append two to three category-specific questions after the fixed six. Examples:

- **Oral care / personal care with claims:** how would you classify each SKU — cosmetic or
  over-the-counter drug — and are you set up to produce both? What documentation comes with a run
  (COA, stability, microbial), and is challenge testing yours or ours?
- **Food and beverage:** co-packer certifications held, allergen handling and changeover, shelf-life
  validation.
- **Supplements:** cGMP certification, label-claim verification testing, and who holds responsibility
  for the claims substantiation file.

Route the regulatory answer out. The manufacturer classifies; a regulatory consultant or counsel
confirms before anything prints. VGP frames the question and names who should answer it.

### The blanks

| Placeholder | What goes there | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| Formats and fill sizes | Physical format and fill per SKU | Founder. Fill size is a decision, not a fact — if unknown, use the current size and flag it as open on the call. Better than a blank. |
| **One specific reason** | One sentence naming why *that* manufacturer | Their own site plus the evaluation notes. This single line separates the email from the fifty templated ones they receive. Never blank, never reused verbatim across two recipients. |
| Volume range | Opening run, and a scale run for the second quote | The engagement's forecast or intake |
| Product brief | The brief the email promises | Built separately — see below |

### Who is copied

Copy the advisor on every thread, or send from the advisor with the founder copied. Two effects:
replies can be compared in real time rather than a week late, and a second name on the thread
signals the brand is operating with support rather than as a one-person shop, which changes how the
inbound is triaged.

### Never send the email before the brief exists

The email promises a written brief. Good manufacturers ask for it the same day. A founder who cannot
produce it has just said they are not ready, and that impression decides which team they get.

## 2 · The follow-up

Five business days later, as a reply on the founder's own thread so the original sits underneath.

```
Hello,

Following up on the note below about contract manufacturing for our <n> <category> SKUs.

If this isn't a fit for your capabilities or your current capacity, just tell me and I'll stop —
no hard feelings and I'd rather know now.

If it is a fit, the fastest path is a short call. I'm flexible this week and next.

Best regards,
<FOUNDER NAME>
```

The line that works is *"just tell me and I'll stop."* An easy exit produces an answer; chasing
produces silence.

**On a no, ask one more question:** *"Is there a manufacturer you'd point me to who does handle
this?"* A manufacturer who cannot take the volume usually knows who can, and an industry referral
moves faster than a cold email.

---

## 3 · The first call

Twenty to thirty minutes. Not a buying conversation and not a pitch — an assessment, and the input
collection for the scorecard. Notes live; scorecard the same day, while the tone is still fresh.

| Ask | Good answer | Worrying answer |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum order quantity | A specific number per SKU, plus a smaller pilot number. Reorder behaviour volunteered. | "It depends." A single large number with no pilot path. |
| Formula ownership | Stated plainly — either the brand owns what it pays to develop, or the manufacturer owns its stock base and the brand owns its customisation. Either is workable when stated. | Vague, deflected, or "we can talk about that later." This is the trap. Get it in writing. |
| Regulatory classification | They classify the SKUs unprompted and describe what changes per bucket. | Not considered, or "it doesn't matter." It matters. |
| Sampling and pilot | A defined process with stated cost and timeline. A fee here is normal and is a positive signal. | Free unlimited samples with no process, or no sampling stage before a full run. |
| Lead time | A range with drivers named — components, testing, production queue. | One optimistic number with no conditions. |
| Documentation | COA, stability, microbial described as standard per run. | Treated as an add-on, or unfamiliar. |

**Three questions that are not on the list:**

1. *"Who would I be working with day to day, and what is their response time?"* The answer predicts
   the next two years.
2. *"Two references from brands my size who launched in the last eighteen months?"* Then call them
   and ask one question: what went wrong, and how did the manufacturer handle it.
3. *"What kills projects like ours at your shop?"* Good manufacturers answer honestly. "Nothing" is
   a sales answer.

**Close every call with:** *"What do you need from me to put a quote in front of me, and when could
I expect it?"* — then stop talking and write down the answer verbatim. It converts a pleasant
conversation into a dated commitment, and a refusal to give a date is itself information.

---

## 4 · The weighted scorecard

Score 1–5 per criterion, multiply by weight, total. The weights below are set for an early brand at
low opening volume with a capacity-constrained founder. Re-weight deliberately for a brand at scale
and say in the document that you have.

| Criterion | Weight | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory & quality posture | 20% | Registration, quality certification, claim-class capability, documentation as standard. The floor, not a differentiator. |
| MOQ & lead time | 20% | At low opening volume this decides whether the relationship is possible at all. A pilot option beats a discount. |
| Category fit | 20% | Do they make this category today, or would they be learning on the founder's money? |
| Cost against target | 15% | Not lowest cost — cost against the landed target the shelf prices imply. Weighted below fit on purpose. |
| Responsiveness | 10% | Pre-customer behaviour is the best available predictor of post-customer behaviour. |
| Capacity to scale | 10% | Can they still serve the brand at 5–10x, or is a second search waiting in a year? |
| Packaging & components | 5% | Sourcing, tooling costs, tooling timelines. |

**Reading the result.** The scorecard does not pick the winner; it prevents picking on charm and
forces the founder to articulate an override. Carry two finalists with live pricing, because the
first choice's timeline will slip. A low cost score with strong regulatory and MOQ scores is usually
right early; a high cost score with a weak MOQ score almost never is. Offshore sample sources are a
cost-and-quality reference point, not a default — weigh them against domestic options on lead time,
freight, regulatory posture and how fast someone answers the phone when a run goes wrong.

## 5 · The product brief

A separate client-facing document, shared with manufacturers **under NDA only**. Sections:

1. Company and contact — brand, category, decision maker, location, current production, channels
   today, channel being opened, advisor as second contact.
2. What we are asking you to quote — SKU table with format, fill size, opening run, scale run.
3. Formulation intent — ingredient posture, actives, exclusions, and **sensory targets** per SKU.
4. Claims — intended claims, substantiation held, substantiation needed, and the classification
   question put to the manufacturer.
5. Packaging and components — primary, closure, secondary, who sources; plus label artwork status,
   barcode status, case pack, shelf-life target.
6. Cost targets — current price, planned price, planning COGS assumption, and target landed cost.
7. Timeline — milestones with target dates and honest status.
8. What we are not sharing — an explicit statement that positioning, channel strategy, pipeline and
   margin model stay with the brand.

**Ship it deliberately unfinished.** Mark every unanswered field `— TO COMPLETE —` inside the
document, not just in the covering note, and tell the founder not to send a marked draft to a
manufacturer. Unfinished-and-labelled is honest and it makes the founder's homework legible.
Finished-looking-but-invented is the failure mode.

**Sensory targets are worth unusual specificity.** Texture, foam, flavour intensity, aftertaste,
scent — these are what make a co-manufactured product feel like someone else's. Cheap to specify up
front, expensive to fix after a run.

---

## Boundaries carried in every build

- **NDA before formulation detail.** A manufacturer who treats that request as an imposition has
  told the founder something useful.
- **Manufacturers receive a manufacturing brief, not a strategy.** Positioning, account pipeline,
  margin model and pricing ladder do not travel.
- **Regulatory, legal and tax questions route out.** Frame the question, name who answers it,
  document that it was routed. Label the deliverable "not legal, tax or regulatory advice."
- **Never invent a figure.** Prices, COGS ranges and volumes carried into the brief must be labelled
  with their source and their status — planning assumption versus verified.
- **Reset dead dates out loud.** When a milestone is unreachable, say so, say where the delay
  actually sat, and carry a real date. A decorative date teaches the founder the plan is theatre.

## Build notes

- House style, Word output: see the document style and builder notes in
  [`docs/prompts/client-engagement-operations.md`](../prompts/client-engagement-operations.md).
- Deliver Word or PDF, never raw Markdown.
- Pair the package with an **action list** naming the founder's items and the advisor's items, in
  dependency order, with the reasoning under each — not just the instruction.

*Derived from contract manufacturer outreach sequences run on VGP engagements in September 2026
across two categories. Contains no client-identifying detail by design.*
